name: Xhosa
notes:
Xhosa (isiXhosa), a Nguni language of South Africa. Related to Zulu; has /r/ unlike Zulu.

CLICKS. Three click types — dental ⟨c⟩ ǀ, lateral ⟨x⟩ ǁ, postalveolar ⟨q⟩ ǃ — each in six series, giving eighteen click consonants: plain ⟨c⟩ [kǀ], aspirated ⟨ch⟩ [kǀʰ], slack-voiced ⟨gc⟩ [ɡǀ], nasal ⟨nc⟩ [ŋǀ], breathy nasal ⟨ngc⟩ [ŋǀ], and nasal-plus-velar ⟨nkc⟩ [ŋkǀ], with the ⟨x⟩ and ⟨q⟩ rows parallel (the six-series click structure is standard in Xhosa click descriptions, e.g. jessen2002_acoustic; full text not consulted). Every click carries a rear (velar) closure, so the two-symbol notation kǀ / ŋǀ is the segment, not a cluster (IPA convention for clicks; the superscript variant ᵏǀ found in some sources writes the same segment). ⟨ngc⟩ and ⟨nc⟩ share a surface symbol here: they differ by the breathy/depressor voice quality of the nasal, which this spec does not transcribe (see DEPRESSORS).

STOPS. ⟨b⟩ is the implosive /ɓ/ and ⟨bh⟩ the slack-voiced plosive /b/ — the pair is a spelling contrast, not an aspiration one. ⟨p t k ts tsh tl kr⟩ are ejective in phonetic realisation ([pʼ tʼ kʼ tsʼ tʃʼ tɬʼ kxʼ]; jessen2002_acoustic measures plosives as more consistently ejective than the corresponding clicks, though full text not consulted) and contrast with the aspirated ⟨ph th kh tyh qh ch xh⟩; the grapheme table states the phonemic plain/aspirated contrast and leaves the ejection to the phonetic layer, exactly as it leaves the depressor voice quality.

PALATALS AND LATERALS. ⟨ty⟩ [c], ⟨tyh⟩ [cʰ], ⟨dy⟩ [ɟ] (written t̠ʲʼ, t̠ʲʰ, d̠ʲʱ in narrower sources). ⟨hl⟩ [ɬ], ⟨dl⟩ [ɮ], ⟨tl⟩ [tɬ] are the lateral obstruents; ⟨dl⟩ is a plain fricative, not an affricate. ⟨rh⟩ is the velar fricative [x] and ⟨kr⟩ the velar affricate [kx]. ⟨h⟩ is [h] and ⟨hh⟩ [ɦ]; [ɦ] is sometimes spelled ⟨h⟩ as well, and the kaikki transcriptions take that reading throughout — the table here follows the spelling contrast the grapheme table draws instead.

POST-NASAL HARDENING. A class 9/10 nasal prefix hardens a following fricative: ⟨nz⟩ is [ndz], and a class 9/10 nasal prefix affricates a following fricative and, if the fricative was voiceless, also makes it ejective in careful speech (claim is standard, e.g. saul_botha2020; full text not consulted), so ⟨mf⟩ is [ɱpf] and ⟨mv⟩ [ɱbv]. Hardening is a property of the class 9/10 nasal only. Under the class 1/3 prefix ⟨um-⟩ the same spelling is a syllabic nasal plus a plain fricative — ⟨imfene⟩ [iɱpfeːne] against ⟨umfana⟩ [um̩faːna] — because that nasal is a syllable, not a prenasalisation (see NASALS).

NASALS. The prenasalised series is written with the nasal letter before the stop — ⟨mb mbh mp mph nd nt ng nk nj nz⟩ — and ⟨mbh⟩ carries the plain [b] of ⟨bh⟩ rather than the implosive of ⟨b⟩, so ⟨umbhobho⟩ is [um̩boːbo]. The slack-voice (depressor) nasals ⟨mh⟩ [m̤], ⟨nh⟩ [n̤], ⟨nyh⟩ [n̠̤ʲ] and ⟨ngh⟩ [ŋ̤] surface here as the plain nasal, on the same grounds as the depressor obstruents (see DEPRESSORS); they still need table entries, or the ⟨h⟩ is emitted as a segment. ⟨ngʼ⟩ is the plain velar nasal [ŋ] against ⟨ng⟩ [ŋɡ].

SYLLABIC NASAL. The class 1/3 prefix ⟨um-⟩ is the Nguni reflex of Proto-Bantu */mu-/ and its nasal is a syllable of its own, while the class 9/10 prefix /iN-/ is a plain prenasalisation: "/m/ is relatively stable, always syllabic [...] Bantu /N/ is generally non-syllabic" (choti2015, p. 37). Xhosa spells the two alike, so the rules key on the one cue the orthography gives — a word-initial ⟨u⟩ immediately before the nasal — which is why ⟨umbala⟩ is [um̩ɓaːla] but ⟨imbali⟩ and ⟨ibumba⟩ keep the prenasalised reading. Kaikki's Xhosa transcriptions mark this nasal as a syllable and also place the penultimate length ON it ([um̩ːzi] for ⟨umzi⟩); this spec marks the syllabicity but still counts nuclei by vowel, so the length lands on the ⟨u⟩ instead.

MULTIGRAPH KEYS ⟨ntl⟩ ⟨nty⟩ ⟨ndy⟩ ⟨ntsh⟩ ⟨ndl⟩ ⟨mhl⟩ exist to defeat maximal munch: without them ⟨nt⟩ and ⟨nd⟩ win and ⟨intloko⟩ comes out with a plain /l/ instead of the lateral affricate. They also record the homorganic place of the nasal before a palatal ([ɲc], [ɲɟ], [ɲtʃ]), which is why ⟨nj⟩ is [ɲdʒ] on the same footing. ⟨mhl⟩ is there for the same reason on the other side: the depressor digraph ⟨mh⟩ would otherwise win a character early and strand the ⟨l⟩ of ⟨umhlaba⟩.

PROSODY. Tone is phonemic (two levels) but is not written; no rule can recover it from the orthography. Measured against the kaikki Xhosa gold, whose IPA column marks tone throughout: 841 of 892 entries carry a tone diacritic, and folding those diacritics out of the gold only (this spec never emits one, so the fold is one-sided) drops PER from 0.3779 to 0.1519 and moves exact match from 2.8% to 41.2% -- see `valid_ceiling` for the citation. Penultimate lengthening IS predictable and is encoded (see the stress block). Words cited in isolation carry a further pre-pausal lengthening, which is why sources transcribe some monosyllables long ([saː], [kǃʰaː]); that is an utterance-level effect and is not encoded, so a monosyllable — having no penult — comes out short.

DEPRESSORS. The slack-voiced obstruents ⟨bh d g v z j dl gc gq gx ngc ngq ngx⟩ lower the pitch of the following vowel and are transcribed in narrow work with a devoicing ring on the consonant and breathy voice on the vowel ([íb̥ǎ̤ːsi] ⟨ibhasi⟩); Jessen & Roux (2002) is the acoustic study. This spec writes the broad voiced symbols and leaves the voice-quality detail to a phonetic layer.

NOT ENCODED: mid-vowel height alternation ([e]~[ɛ], [o]~[ɔ]) conditioned by the following vowel — the phenomenon is real but the kaikki transcriptions mark it in a handful of entries only, so no gold can currently distinguish encoding it from guessing.

sources.author: Larry M. Hyman
sources.title: Penultimate lengthening in Bantu: Analysis and spread
sources.publisher: John Benjamins (Language Typology and Historical Contingency, eds. Bickel, Grenoble, Peterson & Timberlake)
sources.notes: Quotes Doke (1967: 94) on Nguni penultimate stress and length. Its Table 1 shows most of the surveyed Bantu languages, Ndebele included, lengthening monosyllables pre-pausally; Shekgalagari is the exception. The paper therefore supports the penult claim, not a monosyllable exemption.

allophone_rules.notes: ⟨w⟩ after a consonant is secondary rounding on that consonant rather than a separate glide segment — ⟨incwadi⟩ [iŋǀʷaːdi], ⟨umnqweno⟩ [umŋǃʷeːno], ⟨krwe⟩ [kxʷe]; the kaikki transcriptions consistently place the rounding diacritic on the preceding consonant rather than transcribing a separate glide, which is the reading this rule follows.

⟨m⟩ before another consonant is the syllabic nasal /m̩/, the reflex of an older /mu/ prefix: "/m/ is relatively stable, always syllabic" (choti2015, p. 37). The prenasalised ⟨mb mbh mp mph mf mv⟩ are single graphemes and never reach this rule (see XH_UM_PREFIX_SYLLABIC_MB); ⟨m⟩ before a vowel stays a plain onset (⟨umama⟩).

The same syllabic nasal as XH_SYLLABIC_M, stated separately because ⟨mhl⟩ is a single grapheme in the table — it has to be, or the depressor digraph ⟨mh⟩ wins the longest match one character early and strands the ⟨l⟩ — so the nasal is never a phoneme slot of its own for the general rule to see. It fires everywhere, not only after a prefix ⟨u⟩: ⟨namhlanje⟩ and ⟨mhlawumbi⟩ carry the syllabic nasal word-internally and word-initially, which is the behaviour of a nasal that "is relatively stable, always syllabic" (choti2015, p. 37).

The class 1/3 prefix ⟨um-⟩ is the Nguni reflex of Proto-Bantu */mu-/ and its nasal is a syllable of its own, while the class 9/10 prefix /iN-/ is a plain homorganic prenasalisation: "the two nasal prefixes also differ in their phonological behavior in that /m/ is relatively stable, always syllabic, and conditions limited segmental and prosodic alternations [...] Bantu /N/ is generally non-syllabic and triggers a series of segmental and prosodic alternations" (choti2015, p. 37). The two are spelled alike in Xhosa, so the rule keys on the one cue the orthography gives — a word-initial ⟨u⟩ immediately before the nasal. It fires only there, which is why ⟨ibumba⟩ and ⟨igumbi⟩ keep the prenasalised reading. The context reads the ⟨u⟩ grapheme rather than its phoneme: penultimate lengthening (XH_PENULT_LENGTH-equivalent nucleus_stressed) already turns it into "uː" in disyllabic um- words (⟨umfi⟩, ⟨umpu⟩) by the time this rule runs, and a phoneme-keyed condition would silently stop matching there.

⟨mbh⟩ is the prenasalised counterpart of ⟨bh⟩, the plain (non-implosive) [b], so ⟨umbhobho⟩ is [um̩boːbo], not *[um̩ɓoːɓo]. Penultimate lengthening targets the PENULT, so a word-final vowel is never long: ⟨molo⟩ is [moːlo], not *[moːloː], and the monosyllables ⟨fa⟩ and ⟨lo⟩ have no penult to lengthen at all. Undoes the nucleus_stressed lengthening wherever the orthographic syllable count puts the last vowel of the word inside the stressed nucleus (a vowel run such as ⟨oo⟩ is one nucleus spelled with two letters). Isolation forms in the literature are also pre-pausally lengthened (Hyman 2013), an utterance-level effect this spec does not model.

stress.notes: Nguni prominence is penultimate: "Stress in Nguni [Xhosa, Zulu, Swati, Ndebele] is normally on the penultimate syllable which is also normally long" (Doke 1967: 94, quoted in Hyman 2013). The prominence is realised as length rather than as an accentual mark, so stress_mark is empty and the length is written by the nucleus_stressed entries in positional_graphemes. vowel_letters is declared because ⟨y⟩ and ⟨w⟩ are consonants here: without it the bundled syllabifier reads ⟨oya⟩ as one nucleus and the length lands on the wrong vowel, or on two.

kaikki.citation: Xhosa tone is phonemic but never written, and this spec emits no tone diacritics, so the raw PER of 0.3779 against the kaikki Xhosa gold (887 scored entries) measures tone marks the hypothesis could never reproduce, not a spelling defect. Folding tone (combining acute, grave, circumflex, caron, and the grave-acute-grave contour mark) out of the gold IPA only -- one-sided, since the hypothesis side already carries none -- drops PER to 0.1519 and moves exact match from 2.8% to 41.2%; 841 of the 892 kaikki entries carry at least one tone diacritic. Measured against kaikki's Xhosa dump this session, not sourced from a published figure.
